for a linearly-parameterized MDP, the sample complexity is determined by the feature dimension rather than the state-action space size.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show that the curse of dimensionality in tabular MDP can be avoided when the MDP is linearly parameterized.
the curse of dimensionality in RL can be broken by leveraging the structure of MDP, which is a long-standing problem in RL and has attracted much attention recently.

we provide a theoretical foundation to support a practical approach to RL, where the MDP is assumed to admit a linearly-parameterized transition kernel, and the agent has access to a generatively sampled transition data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for RL with a generative model for linearly-parameterized MDPs, model-based approach can achieve a better sample complexity bound than Q-learning, when the number of features is relatively small.

the curse of dimensionality can be avoided by using a generative model to learn the MDP's transition kernel, and this is especially useful when the state-action feature dimension $K$ is much smaller than the state space size.
the sample complexity of RL can scale with the feature dimension $K$ rather than the state space $|\mathcal S|$, which is a desirable property for RL in high-dimensional settings.
